entries.title: Ukraine: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham to visit Kyiv in show of support on Ukraine's Independence Day
entries.summary: Andy Burnham's first trip abroad as PM will see him co-chair a meeting of Ukraine's main backers and meet with Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The visit comes as Ukraine marks its 35th independence day. DW has more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: UK PM Andy Burnham to visit Kyiv in show of support

August 24, 2026

Andy Burnham's first trip abroad as PM will see him co-chair a meeting of Ukraine's main backers and meet with Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The visit comes as Ukraine marks its 35th independence day. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Andy Burnham visits Kyiv on his first overseas trip since becoming the UK's prime minister
  • Burnham is set to co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing and meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
  • Ukraine has been calling for its allies to supply more air defenses and apply more pressure on Russia, which has escalated its attacks on civilians in recent weeks
  • The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence from the Soviet Union
  • The United Nations Security Council is scheduled to hold a special session on Ukraine later on Monday

Here is a roundup of the main developments related to Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, August 24, 2026:

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Thank you for joining us as we bring you updates from the war in Ukraine, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham set to co-chair a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Kyiv on Monday.

The meeting comes as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who is under mounting political pressure at home, has been urging his country's Western allies to increase their air defense supplies amid intensifying Russian airstrikes.

Burnham, who welcomed Zelenskyy to the UK as his first international guest last month, is expected to reassert the UK's support for Ukraine's defense against Russia's invasion.

Burnham's trip, his first outside of the UK since taking office in July, coincides with Ukraine's 35th independence day.

Follow this blog for updates on these stories and more developments from the war in Ukraine.

entries.title: Norway: King Harald's health has 'deteriorated,' palace says
entries.summary: The 89-year-old King of Norway is Europe's oldest reigning monarch. He has been suffering from a blood condition.
entries.content:
Norway

Norway: King Harald's health has 'deteriorated' — palace

August 24, 2026

The 89-year-old King of Norway is Europe's oldest reigning monarch. He has been suffering from a blood condition.

The health of Norway's King Harald has "deteriorated" while in the hospital this weekend, the royal household said in a statement on Sunday.

Harald, 89, is being treated for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by the rapid destruction of red blood cells.

The disorder causes fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath and paleness.

"His Majesty the King's health deteriorated ​over the weekend. The King is ⁠receiving ​antibiotics for ​a bacterial infection in his ​blood, and ‌has responded to this ​treatment," the ⁠palace said. His condition was stable, the statement added.

What else do we know about the health of Norway's king?

Harald was admitted on Monday to Oslo University Hospital because of fluid retention related to cortisone treatment he has been receiving. He was placed on sick leave for two weeks.

The king has also canceled a visit to the Trondelag region in central Norway on September 1 and 2, which fall after the two-week sick leave period.

Several relatives have visited him in hospital on Sunday, including his wife, Queen Sonja, their son Crown Prince Haakon, Haakon's wife Crown Princess Mette-Marit and the king's sister, according to the Verdens Gang newspaper.

Haakon has been acting as regent in his father's absence.

Harald's history of health issues

Harald, who ascended the throne in 1991, is the oldest reigning monarch in Europe.

The king has suffered from numerous health issues in recent years. He has had a pacemaker fitted and has been forced to scale back his official activities and responsibilities.

He was hospitalized with an infection and dehydration in February this year during a private trip with Queen Sonja in Tenerife.

Despite his health issues, he has said he will not abdicate, as he took a lifelong oath before parliament.

Norwegian royals' difficult year

Harald's health is the latest concern for the Norwegian royals, who have been marred by scandal this year.

His son Haakon's wife, Mette-Marit, has been in the headlines for her close ties with late US financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Her son from a previous marriage, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced in June to four years in prison on two counts of rape.

Hoiby has appealed the verdict.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Kazakhstan parliamentary vote cements president's power
entries.summary: Candidates from seven state-approved parties took part in the election, while opposition parties were banned. As Central Asia's largest nation, Kazakhstan maintains a delicate balance between Russia and the West.
entries.content:
Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan parliamentary vote cements president's power

Published August 23, 2026last updated August 23, 2026

Candidates from seven state-approved parties took part in the election, while opposition parties were banned. As Central Asia's largest nation, Kazakhstan maintains a delicate balance between Russia and the West.

Kazakhstan's ruling party comforably won an election for the country's new, single-chamber parliament on Sunday, according to exit polls.

State television shared three exit polls giving the Adilet party between 70% and 72% of the vote.

The vote comes after a new constitution approved in March did away with the Senate to create a new unicameral Kurultai — a reference to the medieval councils of the region's nomadic past.

Backers of the new body say it will give parliament more say in decision making, critics argue it will only cement the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The 73-year-old took the reins from authoritarian Nursultan Nazarbayev — who himself ruled the country for 30 years after the collapse of the Soviet Union — in 2019.

The pro-presidential Adilet party was expected to win an overwhelming majority in Sunday's vote, while exit polls showed four smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also won seats in the new parliament.

Seven state-approved parties have been allowed to field candidates for the 145-seat parliament while genuine opposition parties have been banned.

The election took place amid soaring inflation (which is hovering around 10.2%) and rising taxes, fueling concerns for the government — and particularly Tokayev — of a repeat of January 2022 cost of living unrest that left 238 protesters and police dead.

Press crackdown and financial strain color Kazakhstan's election

Beyond financial strain, Sunday's vote also took place against the background of crackdowns on press freedom, with numerous reporters under house arrest and official criminal cases being brought against 10 independent journalists and bloggers.

Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who worked at the UN, touted his reforms and justified the many changes he has initiated — including the introduction of the new constitution — as necessary in a fast-changing world.

"Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country's history," said Tokayev on Friday.

"Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state," he added.

Tokayev has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow — with their shared Soviet ties — and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Resource-rich and strategically located Kazakhstan also has ties to China and the European Union.

Although Tokayev has said that he has no plans of staying in power beyond his current term, the constitutional reform that 87% of voters backed this March effectively reset term limits for the office — making him eligible to run for another seven-year stint in 2029 should he change his mind.

Edited by: Natalie Muller and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Zelenskyy repeats Ukraine not behind Nord Stream attack
entries.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was assisting German authorities with their investigation into the Nord Stream explosions. A second Ukrainian national was arrested in connection with the blasts.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Zelenskyy repeats Ukraine not behind Nord Stream attack

August 23, 2026

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was assisting German authorities with their investigation into the Nord Stream explosions. A second Ukrainian national was arrested in connection with the blasts.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reiterated on Sunday that Ukraine was not involved in the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream underwater gas pipelines.

"Ukraine has never officially taken part in any operation related to the blowing up of Nord Stream," Zelenskyy told reporters on Sunday in response to a question about the ongoing investigation.

He said that Germany was "well aware that Ukraine did not stand behind the execution or the very conception of this operation."

Zelenskyy hopes 'not to lose trust'

German authorities alleged last month that the attack had been ordered by the Ukrainian state, while a second Ukrainian national was also detained over the blasts this week.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was assisting German authorities with their investigation.

"It is very important for us not to lose our partnership, not to lose the trust of European countries that have been helping Ukraine since the very beginning of this war," he said.

German authorities implicate Ukraine

The Nord Stream 1 pipeline ran under the Baltic Sea and delivered gas from Russia to Germany and other countries in Europe. A second pipeline called Nord Stream 2 was constructed but never went into use.

In September 2022, both pipelines were sabotaged with undersea explosions. No group claimed responsibility for the attack.

In early 2026, German authorities detained the first suspect, a Ukrainian national Serhii K., and alleged that he and six accomplices had acted "on the orders of state authorities in Ukraine."

Prosecutors said the plan was to "destroy the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipelines" with the objective of "permanently halting gas supplies via the pipelines and preventing Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war efforts."

entries.title: Greece: Migrants clash with police at detention center
entries.summary: Clashes broke out between police and people at a migrant detention center in northern Greece, with 35 having escaped the facility before half of them were detained again.
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

Clashes broke out between police and people at a migrant detention center in northern Greece, with 35 having escaped the facility before half of them were detained again.

Migrants clashed with police at a detention center in northern Greece, with 35 having escaped the premises after cutting through a perimeter fence before police detained about half of them again, authorities said on Sunday.

Greece is a major point of entry for migrants to Europe, and the country's conservative prime minister has introduced tough rules to deport those who've been denied asylum in the country.

Greece, along with other European Union countries, for example, is in talks with African countries about establishing centers for failed asylum-seekers, a move that has drawn criticism from international rights groups.

Police deploy flashbangs during clashes

Police said they called for reinforcement to the detention center in Sintiki, a few kilometers from the Bulgarian border, after migrants threw rocks at police.

Authorities used flash-bang grenades against people during those clashes, which they said lasted until the early hours of Sunday morning.

At least five migrants were injured and taken to the hospital. Police recaptured 17 of those who escaped and the search continued for 18 others.

The temporary accommodation center houses about 450 people while their applications are processed, a protracted procedure that can take a long time.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Guinea: Garbage collapse at landfill kills dozens
entries.summary: Heavy seasonal rains caused a mound of garbage to collapse, burying dozens of people and nearby homes before the break of dawn.
entries.content:
Guinea

Guinea: Garbage collapse at landfill kills dozens

August 23, 2026

Heavy seasonal rains caused a mound of garbage to collapse, burying dozens of people and nearby homes before the break of dawn.

At least 30 people have died after a landfill collapsed in Guinea's capital, Conakry, officials said on Sunday.

Heavy rains overnight caused a large mound of rubbish to collapse at the Dar Es Salam landfill, burying nearby homes before dawn.

At least six other people were seriously injured.

Guinea's minister for territorial administration, Djenabou Toure, visited the site, where workers used excavators to search for more bodies.

Landfill was slated for closure

The government had recently ordered the expulsion of nearby residents in informal housing due to a fear of collapses.

Balde Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the Military Engineering Battalion, said the Dar Es Salam site had been slated for closure on Sunday.

Heavy seasonal rains have been known to trigger collapses at landfills in some countries, with Uganda and Ethiopia suffering similar tragedies in recent years. 

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Iran: President defends deal with US as best option for peace
entries.summary: Iran's president has said the country's economy needs a peace deal to attract investors. The Foreign Ministry said Pakistan's top army official will visit Tehran Monday as Islamabad seeks to mediate a resolution.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran: President defends US deal as best option for peace

August 23, 2026

Iran's president has said the country's economy needs a peace deal to attract investors. The Foreign Ministry said Pakistan's top army official will visit Tehran Monday as Islamabad seeks to mediate a resolution.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday defended Tehran's expired Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the United States as the best option for ending hostilities between the two nations, which Pezeshkian described as being "neither war nor peace."

Pezeshkian said members of Iran's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) agreed with the assessment on the basis of, "dignity, wisdom and national interest."

"There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation," Pezeshkian said in remarks published by state-run news agency IRNA. "The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path."

The MoU, signed by US President Donald Trump in June, laid out a 60-day timeline for ending the US-Israeli-led conflict as well as ensuring that Iran give up its nuclear ambitions.

The deadline passed last week with no signs of compromise by either side, and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran closed in response to US-Israeli attacks, putting the global economy in a chokehold for the past six months — still unresolved.

On Sunday, Pezeshkian called it imperative that Iran exit this stalled phase of the conflict to unlock foreign investment to the country.

"Capital and money are extremely sensitive to risk," he said. "We have to remove this risk from the country."

Pakistani mediator expected in Tehran as hardliner warns neighbors not to help US

Iran's Foreign Ministry on Sunday announced that Pakistan's top military leader, Asim Munir, will travel to Iran on Monday.

The visit is part of "Pakistan's ongoing efforts to help consolidate peace and security in the region," Tehran said.

Pakistan was instrumental in getting the MoU between Washington and Tehran signed.

Earlier this month, Islamabad signed its own regional security cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, which observers read as an attempt to counter Iranian influence in the region.

Still, despite news of Munir's travels and Pezeshkian's announcement that the SNSC backs the MoU, that body's new hardline leader, Mohsen Rezaei, warned neighboring countries against aiding the US war effort, saying, "If [Trump] wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner."

Rezaei said Iran would target oil-shipping routes out of the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz — if neighbors join the US economic war against Iran.

entries.title: Could Russia's growing fuel crisis help end the Ukraine war?
entries.summary: Empty pumps, long waits: Attacks on oil refineries have left Russia increasingly short of fuel. Dissident Russian economists say growing anger about shortages among ordinary Russians could help end the Ukraine war.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Could Russia's growing fuel crisis help end the Ukraine war?

August 23, 2026

Empty pumps, long waits: Attacks on oil refineries have left Russia increasingly short of fuel. Dissident Russian economists say growing anger about shortages among ordinary Russians could help end the Ukraine war.

Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries have triggered a new fuel crisis in Russia.

Reuters news agency reports that at least 30 regions are now affected. Unlike the previous wave of shortages, which began in late May and lasted until mid-July, the current crisis is particularly affecting Moscow and the surrounding area, as is apparent from posts on social media. The gas station chains Gazprom Neft and Tatneft have already restricted the sale of fuel in the capital.

"You can't say there isn't any fuel. But it's obvious there's a crisis," says Oleg Grigorenko, editor-in-chief of the Russian independent media portal 7x7, which Russia has branded a "foreign agent." "It's not just a personal problem if you leave the city and don't know whether you can get back again, for example. It's also an economic problem,"

Grigorenko reports that in several regions taxi drivers, courier services and the construction industry are already losing business, as many of their supply chains are fuel-dependent. "The logistics of private construction companies is heavily reliant on gasoline," Grigorenko explains.

People are also having to queue for hours at gas stations in the southern Russian region of Krasnodar, according to local media. The authorities are blaming this on a supposed increase in demand during the holiday period.

But many locals are saying that this summer season is a disaster. Real estate agent Igor Zakharchenko, from Sochi on the Black Sea coast, wrote on Instagram: "With its quiet atmosphere and leisurely pace of life, Sochi today is reminiscent of the time before the Olympic Games, when there were still not many cars on the roads and the city had far fewer holidaymakers and inhabitants. But the thing is: There's no gas in Sochi."

Poor quality fuel

Speaking on the Russian broadcaster RTVI, Igor Ananskikh, first deputy chairman of the energy committee in the Russian parliament, said he expected the gas supply situation to normalize within two to three weeks.

Economist Nikolai Korzhenevsky says this is unlikely. He left Russia in protest at Moscow's war  against Ukraine and now lives abroad. In an interview with DW, he highlighted the worsening quality of fuel in Russia. Acquaintances had sent him photos of their cars displaying error messages that indicate engine damage caused by impurities in the fuel.

"The car won't start and has to go to the garage. The same people are telling me garages have waitlists of several months, even in Moscow," Korzhenevsky says. "And then you have to wait again for months for replacement parts. Obviously some vehicles can't handle the gasoline that's being put in their tanks."

He sees the ongoing problems in the oil and gas industry as harbingers of a much larger and lasting crisis.

Russia's oil exports have fallen more sharply during the war than ever before, Bloomberg news has reported. Oil production has also dropped.

"In 2019, Russia produced 11.5 million barrels per day," says Korzhenevsky. "Today it's less than 9 million. If this trend continues, and the problems with oil refining get worse, production may fall to 8 million barrels. That would create the conditions for a complete economic and systemic crisis."

He doesn't see any quick solution to these problems. In fact he sees Russia going down a similar route to Venezuela, an economy with national income in chronic decline.

Hoping for imports is illusory

The Russian authorities propose to remedy the fuel shortages with imports from India, China or other countries. But Vyacheslav Shiryaev, a Russian business journalist who also now lives abroad, says this is not viable.

Given Russia's current isolation, it's impossible to ensure a daily supply of 200,000 tonnes of fuel, which is the approximate amount of gasoline and diesel Russia needs every day, he told DW. Shiryaev, who publicly opposed the war in Ukraine, is also on the Russian authorities' list of so-called "foreign agents."

Another Russian economist on that list is Igor Lipsits. He told DW that the damaged refineries cannot quickly be restored and will be vulnerable to further air attacks.

This, he says, is why the authorities are already restricting fuel consumption. Municipal services vehicles — medical and rescue workers, police, firefighters — are allowed to jump the line and fill up and so are security personnel and the authorities.

"This is happening in front of people who've waited for hours and it's causing a lot of resentment," says Lipsits, a Kremlin critic who left his teaching post at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow because of increasing political pressure. He too now lives in exile in Europe.

To Lipsits, the current developments in Russia are strongly reminiscent of the collapse of the Soviet Union.

"There were special supply systems for the elite, their own shops and warehouses where they could buy everything they wanted without much difficulty, without waiting in line, and at relatively low prices. That made Russians very angry," he recounts. "When Boris Yeltsin announced that he was going to abolish these closed distribution centers, the people enthusiastically supported him. We are now in a similar situation."

Lipsits says a closed system for fuel distribution is evolving in Russia that will make it a luxury to be able to drive a car.

The key to ending the war?

The economist Shiryaev believes Ukrainian attacks on Russian targets that serve both a military and a civilian purpose could cripple the Russian economy and hasten the end of the war. He believes it would end in just a few weeks if the West supported Ukraine in doubling or tripling the intensity of its attacks.

"Ukraine could bring about disorganization and chaos in the Russian interior, resulting in a total loss of control,"Shiryaev says.

He also thinks the fuel shortage could have a decisive role in undermining the stability of Vladimir Putin's regime.

"If there's no diesel, Russia's 6,000-kilometer railway network comes to a halt," he says. "It could also cripple hundreds of factories and businesses. Without diesel, tens of thousands of trucks would be unable to run, food wouldn't get to the stores, and farmers wouldn't be able to harvest their crops."

Shiryaev says all this could result in curtailing Putin's plans to continue the war.

"If Ukraine destroys the whole oil refining infrastructure, Putin will find that, when he gives an order, it isn't implemented," the economist predicts. Everything will grind to a halt for lack of fuel.

This article was originally written in Russian.

entries.title: Congo, M23 rebels agree to peace roadmap
entries.summary: Negotiators representing the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have agreed to a roadmap for peace. The US State Department, a mediator, released a joint statement.
entries.content:
Democratic Republic of Congo

Congo, M23 rebels agree to peace roadmap

August 23, 2026

Negotiators representing the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have agreed to a roadmap for peace. The US State Department, a mediator, released a joint statement.

After days of negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, representatives from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23 have agreed to a shared roadmap designed to facilitate peace in the DRC after years of brutal war. 

The US State Department, which was involved in mediating talks alongside the African Union (AU), Switzerland and Qatar, released a statement describing the situation on Saturday evening.

The State Department said the agreement builds on a US-brokered deal signed last November in Doha, Qatar, adding that Congo and the rebels had "developed a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement."

Despite a ceasefire being in place since November 15, the shift to peace has been slow, though prisoners, for instance, were recently exchanged.

The newly agreed roadmap made clear that an observer mission monitoring the ceasefire will receive support from UN MONUSCO peacekeeping forces and that further negotiations designed to bring about lasting peace will take place soon.

Hundreds of civilians have been killed and millions displaced by fighting between the two sides since early 2022, when M23 — with backing from neighboring Rwanda — began its quest for control of resource-rich eastern Congo and its gold, cassiterite, coltan and diamonds.

M23, which is accused of committing brutal wartime atrocities, has controlled large swaths of the North and South Kivu provinces since 2025.

The State Department statement released on Saturday said both sides had thanked mediators "for their steadfast support in advancing peace and stability in eastern DRC and the broader Great Lakes region."

entries.title: Harry Kane named footballer of the year in Germany
entries.summary: Harry Kane has added another honor after a remarkable season for Bayern Munich and a strong World Cup with England. Bayern also took the top prize in coaching, and the club's Giulia Gwinn won women's Player of the Year.
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

Harry Kane has added another honor after a remarkable season for Bayern Munich and a strong World Cup with England. Bayern also took the top prize in coaching, and the club's Giulia Gwinn won women's Player of the Year.

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has been named men's Player of the Year in Germany after a record-breaking season for the Bundesliga champions.

Bayern coach Vincent Kompany was voted trainer of the year, while Germany defender Giulia Gwinn completed a clean sweep for the Munich club by winning the women's Player of the Year award.

"A Bayern double — never before have the men and women's Player of the Year awards gone to the same club. Congratulations to Harry and Giulia, as well as our coach Vincent," Bayern president Herbert Hainer said in a club statement. "When men's and women's football makes history together, then that's Bayern, making a mark. We're proud of this result."

Why was Harry Kane named Germany's footballer of the year?

Kane received 272 votes from members of the Association of German Sports Journalists, comfortably ahead of Bayern teammate Michael Olise on 203.

Stuttgart and Germany striker Deniz Undav finished third with 61 votes.

England captain Kane scored 61 goals in 51 competitive appearances for Bayern last season.

"It was the best season of my career so far," Kane said last week after winning the European Golden Shoe for the second time.

His club form was followed by another strong World Cup run with England, where he scored six goals as the team reached the semifinals. Kane also became England's all-time leading scorer at World Cups, taking his overall tournament tally to 14.

The 33-year-old was also awarded the European Golden Shoe for the second time in his career after finishing as the continent's leading league goalscorer.

Former Bayern striker Luca Toni said Kane also deserved to win the Ballon d'Or, football's leading individual award.

Kompany takes coach of the year, Gwinn wins women's award

Kompany was the clear winner among coaches, receiving 314 votes after guiding Bayern to a league and cup double.

Freiburg coach Julian Schuster, who won the award last year, finished second with 87 votes, while Stuttgart's Sebastian Hoeneß was third with 53.

Schuster praised Kompany's work, saying the Belgian was not only a good coach but also made those around him better.

Gwinn won the women's award outright after sharing first place with goalkeeper Ann-Katrin Berger last year.

"This is an honor and a validation of my journey," Gwinn said.

The 27-year-old Bayern defender received 106 votes, narrowly beating teammate Klara Bühl on 94.
